paragraphs: Of course, I will not pretend to be surprised that M. Valdemar’s extraordinary case has caused so much discussion. It would have been a miracle if it had not, especially in the circumstances. Everyone involved wanted to keep the affair from the public, at least for the present, until we had more opportunities to investigate. Our efforts to do so allowed a confused or exaggerated account to circulate, producing many unpleasant misrepresentations and, quite naturally, a great deal of disbelief.
It has now become necessary for me to give the facts, as far as I understand them myself. Briefly, they are these:

Over the last three years, my attention had repeatedly been drawn to mesmerism. About nine months ago, it suddenly struck me that the experiments conducted so far contained a remarkable and utterly inexplicable omission: no one had yet been mesmerized at the point of death. Three things remained to be discovered. First, could a patient in that condition respond at all to the magnetic influence? Second, if so, did the condition weaken or strengthen that response? Third, to what extent, or for how long, could the process stop the advance of Death? There were other questions to investigate, but these most excited my curiosity, especially the last, because of its immensely important consequences.

As I looked for someone on whom I could test these questions, I thought of my friend M. Ernest Valdemar, the well-known compiler of the “Legal Library,” and author, under the pen name Issachar Marx, of the Polish versions of “Wallenstein” and “Gargantua.” M. Valdemar has lived mainly in Harlem, N.Y., since 1839. He is—or was—particularly noticeable for his extreme thinness, his legs closely resembling John Randolph’s, and for the whiteness of his whiskers, which contrasted sharply with his black hair. As a result, people commonly mistook the hair for a wig. His temperament was distinctly nervous, making him a good subject for mesmeric experiments. On two or three occasions I had put him to sleep with little difficulty, but the other results disappointed me. His unusual constitution had naturally led me to expect more. His will was never definitely or entirely under my control, and I could obtain no reliable results from him in clairvoyance. I always blamed these failures on his poor health. Some months before I met him, his doctors had diagnosed established tuberculosis. Indeed, he habitually spoke calmly about his approaching death, as something neither to be avoided nor regretted.

When the ideas I have mentioned first occurred to me, it was naturally M. Valdemar who came to mind. I knew his steady philosophical attitude too well to fear objections from him. He had no relatives in America likely to interfere. I spoke frankly to him about the subject, and to my surprise he seemed intensely interested. I say “to my surprise” because, although he had always willingly submitted to my experiments, he had never before shown any interest in what I did. His disease was of a kind that allowed the time of death to be calculated exactly. We finally agreed that he would send for me about twenty-four hours before the time his doctors predicted he would die.
A little more than seven months ago, I received the following note from M. Valdemar himself:
MY DEAR P——,
You may as well come now. D—— and F—— agree that I cannot last beyond midnight tomorrow. I think they have calculated the time very nearly.
VALDEMAR

I received the note within half an hour of its being written, and fifteen minutes later I was in the dying man’s room. I had not seen him for ten days, and the dreadful change in so short a time appalled me. His face was lead-gray. His eyes had no brightness at all. He was so wasted that his cheekbones had broken through the skin. He was coughing up enormous amounts of sputum. His pulse was barely detectable. Yet, remarkably, he retained his mental faculties and some physical strength. He spoke clearly, took medicines to ease his symptoms without help, and when I entered was writing notes in pencil in a pocketbook. Pillows propped him up in bed. Doctors D—— and F—— were attending him.

After squeezing Valdemar’s hand, I took the doctors aside and obtained a detailed account of his condition. For eighteen months, the left lung had been partly bone-like or gristly, and was of course entirely useless in sustaining life. The upper part of the right lung was also partly, if not completely, hardened into bone, while the lower part was nothing but a mass of pus-filled nodules merging into one another. There were several large holes, and at one point the lung had permanently stuck to the ribs. These changes in the right lobe were fairly recent. The hardening had advanced unusually fast. A month earlier, there had been no sign of it, and the attachment to the ribs had been noticed only within the past three days. Besides tuberculosis, the patient was suspected of having an aneurysm in the aorta, but the bone-like symptoms made an exact diagnosis impossible. Both doctors believed that M. Valdemar would die around midnight the following day, Sunday. It was then seven o’clock on Saturday evening.

When Doctors D—— and F—— left the patient’s bedside to speak with me, they had said their final goodbyes to him. They had not intended to return, but at my request they agreed to look in on him at about ten the following night.

After they left, I spoke freely with M. Valdemar about his approaching death and, more particularly, the proposed experiment. He still declared himself entirely willing, even eager, to undergo it, and urged me to begin at once. A male nurse and a female nurse were attending him. But if something suddenly went wrong, I did not feel comfortable carrying out such a task with no more reliable witnesses than these two might prove to be. I therefore postponed the experiment until about eight the next evening, when a medical student I knew, Mr. Theodore L—l, arrived and removed that difficulty. I had originally intended to wait for the doctors. But M. Valdemar’s urgent pleas, and my conviction that I had no time to lose because he was clearly sinking fast, persuaded me to proceed.
Mr. L—l kindly agreed to my request that he take notes of everything that happened. Most of what I am about to relate is either condensed from his notes or copied word for word.

At about five minutes to eight, I took the patient’s hand and asked him to tell Mr. L—l, as clearly as he could, whether he, M. Valdemar, was entirely willing for me to try mesmerizing him in his present condition.
He answered weakly but quite audibly, “Yes, I want to be mesmerized,” then immediately added, “I’m afraid you’ve left it too long.”

As he spoke, I began the hand movements I had previously found most effective in bringing him under my influence. The first sideways sweep of my hand across his forehead clearly affected him. But although I exerted all my powers, I could produce no further visible effect until a few minutes after ten, when Doctors D—— and F—— arrived as arranged. I briefly explained my plan. They raised no objection, saying the patient was already in his final death struggle. I continued without hesitation, but changed from sideways sweeps to downward ones and fixed my gaze entirely on the suffering man’s right eye.
By now his pulse could no longer be felt. He breathed with a harsh, snoring sound, at intervals of half a minute.

His condition remained almost unchanged for fifteen minutes. Then a natural but very deep sigh came from the dying man’s chest, and the harsh breathing stopped. That is, the harsh sound disappeared; the intervals between breaths did not shorten. His hands and feet were icy cold.

At five minutes to eleven, I saw unmistakable signs of the mesmeric influence. The glassy rolling of his eye changed to an expression of uneasy inward concentration, seen only in the waking sleep of a trance and impossible to mistake. A few quick sideways sweeps of my hand made his eyelids tremble as though he were falling asleep. A few more closed them completely. I was not satisfied with that. After arranging his limbs in an apparently comfortable position, I continued the movements vigorously, exerting my will to the utmost, until his limbs became completely rigid. His legs were fully extended, his arms almost so, resting on the bed a moderate distance from his hips. His head was raised very slightly.

By the time I had done this, it was midnight. I asked the gentlemen present to examine M. Valdemar. After a few tests, they acknowledged that he was in an unusually complete mesmeric trance. Both doctors were intensely curious. Dr. D—— decided at once to stay with the patient all night. Dr. F—— left, promising to return at daybreak. Mr. L—l and the nurses stayed.

We left M. Valdemar entirely undisturbed until about three in the morning. When I approached him, I found him exactly as he had been when Dr. F—— left. He lay in the same position. His pulse was undetectable. His breathing was gentle, scarcely noticeable unless a mirror was held to his lips. His eyes were naturally closed, and his limbs were as rigid and cold as marble. Yet his general appearance was certainly not that of death.

As I approached M. Valdemar, I made a half-hearted attempt to make his right arm follow mine, moving my own gently back and forth above his body. I had never entirely succeeded in this experiment with him before, and certainly had little expectation of succeeding now. To my astonishment, however, his arm readily, though feebly, followed every movement I directed with mine. I decided to risk a few words of conversation.

“M. Valdemar,” I said, “are you asleep?” He did not answer, but I noticed his lips tremble, so I repeated the question again and again. At the third repetition, a very slight shudder passed through his whole body. His eyelids opened far enough to show a white line of the eyeball. His lips moved sluggishly, and in a barely audible whisper came the words:
“Yes—asleep now. Don’t wake me! Let me die like this!”
I felt his limbs and found them as rigid as before. His right arm still followed my hand. I questioned the entranced man again:
“Do you still feel pain in your chest, M. Valdemar?”
This time the answer came immediately, but was even fainter than before:
“No pain—I am dying.”

I thought it best not to disturb him further just then. Nothing more was said or done until Dr. F—— arrived a little before sunrise. He was astonished beyond measure to find the patient still alive. After feeling for a pulse and holding a mirror to his lips, he asked me to speak to the entranced man again. I said:
“M. Valdemar, are you still asleep?”

As before, several minutes passed before he answered. During that time, the dying man seemed to gather his strength to speak. At my fourth repetition of the question, he said very faintly, almost inaudibly:
“Yes; still asleep—dying.”

The doctors now believed—or rather wished—that M. Valdemar should be left undisturbed in his apparently peaceful condition until death came. Everyone agreed that this must now happen within a few minutes. I decided, however, to speak to him once more, simply repeating my earlier question.

As I spoke, the entranced man’s face changed dramatically. His eyes slowly rolled open, the pupils disappearing upward. His skin took on a corpse-like color, resembling white paper rather than parchment. The sharply defined circles of feverish red in the center of each cheek went out all at once. I use that expression because their sudden disappearance reminded me of nothing so much as a candle being blown out. At the same time, his upper lip twisted away from the teeth it had completely covered. His lower jaw dropped with an audible jerk, leaving his mouth wide open and fully exposing his swollen, blackened tongue. I imagine everyone present was familiar with the horrors of a deathbed. Yet M. Valdemar looked so inconceivably hideous at that moment that we all shrank back from the bed.
I feel I have now reached the point in this account where every reader will be startled into outright disbelief. My duty, however, is simply to continue.

There was no longer the faintest sign of life in M. Valdemar. Concluding that he was dead, we were leaving him in the nurses’ care when we noticed his tongue vibrating violently. This continued for perhaps a minute. Then, from the stretched, motionless jaws came a voice that it would be madness for me to try to describe. Two or three words might describe parts of it. I might say, for instance, that the sound was harsh, broken, and hollow. But the hideous whole is indescribable, simply because no similar sound has ever jarred on human ears. Still, there were two features that I thought then, and still think, fairly characterize its tone and convey some idea of its unearthly strangeness. First, the voice seemed to reach our ears—at least mine—from an immense distance, or from some deep cavern within the earth. Second, it affected me—I fear I cannot make myself understood—as jelly-like or sticky substances affect the sense of touch.

I have spoken of both “sound” and “voice.” What I mean is that the syllables were distinct—indeed, astonishingly, chillingly distinct. M. Valdemar spoke, clearly answering the question I had put to him a few minutes earlier. You will remember that I had asked whether he was still asleep. He now said:
“Yes—no—I have been sleeping—and now—now—I am dead.”

No one present even pretended to deny, or tried to suppress, the unspeakable, shuddering horror that those few words, spoken in that way, were so capable of producing. Mr. L—l, the student, fainted. The nurses immediately left the room and could not be persuaded to return. I will not pretend I can make the reader understand my own feelings. For nearly an hour, in silence, without speaking a single word, we worked to revive Mr. L—l. When he regained consciousness, we returned to examining M. Valdemar’s condition.

He remained exactly as I have just described, except that the mirror no longer showed any sign of breathing. We tried unsuccessfully to draw blood from his arm. I should also mention that this arm no longer obeyed my will. I tried in vain to make it follow my hand. In fact, the only real sign of mesmeric influence left was the vibrating movement of his tongue whenever I asked him a question. He seemed to try to answer but no longer had enough willpower. He appeared entirely unaware of questions asked by anyone else, although I tried to establish a mesmeric connection between him and each person present. I believe I have now related everything necessary to understand his condition at that time. We obtained other nurses, and at ten o’clock I left the house with the two doctors and Mr. L—l.

That afternoon, we all returned to see the patient. His condition was exactly the same. We discussed whether waking him would be proper or possible, but readily agreed that it would serve no useful purpose. It was clear that, so far, mesmerism had halted death—or what is usually called death. We all believed that waking M. Valdemar would merely ensure his immediate death, or at least his rapid death.

From that time until the end of last week, nearly seven months, we visited M. Valdemar’s house every day. Sometimes medical friends and others accompanied us. Throughout that time, the man in his waking sleep remained exactly as I have last described him. The nurses attended him constantly.

Last Friday, we finally decided to experiment with waking him, or attempting to wake him. The perhaps unfortunate result of that final experiment has caused so much private discussion and so much public emotion that I cannot help considering unjustified.

To bring M. Valdemar out of his mesmeric trance, I used the customary hand movements. For a while, they had no effect. The first sign of revival was a slight downward movement of the iris. We noticed something especially remarkable: as the pupil lowered, a yellowish fluid poured from beneath the eyelids, with a sharp, intensely foul smell.
Someone now suggested that I try influencing the patient’s arm as before. I tried and failed. Dr. F—— then indicated that he wanted me to ask a question. I asked:
“M. Valdemar, can you explain what you feel or wish for now?”

The feverish circles returned to his cheeks at once. His tongue quivered—or rather rolled violently in his mouth, though his jaws and lips remained rigid as before. At last, the same hideous voice I have described burst out:
“For God’s sake! Quick! Quick! Put me to sleep—or, quick! Wake me! Quick! I tell you that I am dead!”

I was utterly shaken, and for a moment could not decide what to do. First I tried to settle the patient back into his trance. But the will had stopped functioning completely, and the attempt failed. I reversed the process and struggled just as earnestly to wake him. I soon saw that this attempt would succeed—or at least I soon imagined it would succeed completely. I am sure everyone in the room expected the patient to wake.
But no human being could possibly have been prepared for what actually happened.

As I rapidly made the mesmeric hand movements, cries of “dead! dead!” burst from the suffering man’s tongue, not his lips. His entire body at once—within a single minute, or even less—shrank, crumbled, absolutely rotted away beneath my hands. On the bed, in front of everyone present, lay a nearly liquid mass of loathsome, revolting decay.
